```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(ggplot2)
  library(knitr)
})

kOutputDir <- file.path("..", "output", "omip39")

ReadOutput <- function(name) {
  path <- file.path(kOutputDir, name)
  if (!file.exists(path)) {
    stop(
      "The analysis output is missing: ", path, "\n",
      "Run every script from 02 to 05 first. See the section 'Reproducing this'."
    )
  }
  read.csv(path, check.names = FALSE)
}

OutputImage <- function(name) {
  file.path(kOutputDir, name)
}
```

## Why this dataset

The PBMC report showed that an automated template gates a whole experiment from
one text file. What it did not show was whether the template lands where an
expert lands, because there was nothing to compare against. OMIP-39 fixes that.
It is a published panel for human adaptive NKG2C+ natural killer cells [1], and
its FlowRepository deposit ships the FlowJo workspace that the authors used, so
the manual result does not come from this project. The same donor file is gated
twice, once by the authors in FlowJo and once here by an openCyto template, and
the two frequencies sit side by side.

The deposit also ships twelve single stained controls, so the analysis computes
compensation from scratch instead of taking it from the file. That computation
turned out to be the part with the finding in it.

The report has five parts. They are compensation computed from the controls,
automated gating from a template, that template compared against the published
manual gates, the paper's own claims tested against the deposited data, and
clustering as a third route to the same populations.

```{r}
#| label: dataset

match_table <- ReadOutput("control_match_table.csv")
kable(
  match_table[, c("stain", "channel", "marker", "matched_by")],
  caption = "The twelve compensation controls, each matched to the channel it stains."
)
```

## Part 1: compensation

### Matching controls to channels

Every control file carries one stain, and that stain names one detector in the
panel. FlowJo makes a person do this matching in its interface, while here the
matching is derived from the marker names that the FCS files already carry. The
matcher runs four passes, and each pass exists because a real file broke the
pass before it.

```{r}
#| label: match-passes

passes <- as.data.frame(table(match_table$matched_by))
colnames(passes) <- c("pass", "controls")
kable(passes, caption = "How many controls each matching pass resolved.")
```

Read the passes as a ladder of tolerance. `exact` compares the two strings
character for character, and `normalised` ignores case and punctuation.
`collapsed` removes every separator, which is what resolves `CD2 PerCP-Cy55` on
the control against `CD2 PerCPCy55` in the panel. `antibody` matches on the
antibody name alone and ignores the fluorochrome, which is what resolves
`Zombie auqa CD14 CD19` against `Zombie aqua CD14 CD19`. That last pair is a
typo in the panel. Because the matcher reports which pass it used, a weaker
match is visible rather than silent.

### Whether each control can support an estimate

A spillover value is a ratio between the signal a fluorochrome puts into its own
detector and the signal it puts into another one, and both terms need a positive
population to measure. A bead control is almost entirely positive. A cell
control is not, because a marker that sits on a minority of cells leaves most
events negative.

```{r}
#| label: control-quality

quality <- ReadOutput("control_quality.csv")
kable(
  quality[, c("stain", "positive_percent", "primary_is_brightest", "verdict")],
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Percentage of positive events per control, against a threshold set at the 99.9th percentile of the unstained control.",
  col.names = c("Control", "Positive, percent", "Brightest on its own detector", "Verdict")
)
```

Two results come out of this table. Every control reads brightest on the
detector it was matched to, so the matching above is correct and the channel
assignment is not the problem anywhere in this dataset. Four controls are
positive on under 20 percent of their events, with NKp30 positive on 3.5 percent
and NKG2C on 7.0 percent. Those two values are real biology, because NKG2C marks
a small adaptive NK subset and that subset is the point of the paper. The two
controls are still poor compensation controls.

### The finding: mode against median

`flowStats::spillover_ng()` defaults to `method = "mode"`. On a bead control the
mode is the positive peak, because nearly every event is positive. On a cell
control for a rare marker the mode is the negative peak, and the ratio it
produces does not describe spillover at all. This behaviour was not obvious from
the code. It appeared as a spillover value of 164 percent, which is not physical
for that pair, so the cause had to be found.

The measurement below runs the computation under every combination of the three
relevant arguments, and it scores each result against the matrix that the
instrument stored for this experiment. The stored matrix is a fair reference. It
was built from these same controls, by the acquisition software, with an
operator who checked it.

```{r}
#| label: method-sweep

sweep <- ReadOutput("method_sweep.csv")
kable(
  sweep,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Every configuration, scored against the stored matrix. Differences are in percentage points.",
  col.names = c("method", "pregate", "normFilter", "channels",
                "max difference", "median difference", "values above 100 percent",
                "correlation", "status")
)
```

Read the first row and the third row against each other. Both pregate and both
filter, and only the summary statistic differs. The mode gives a correlation of
0.619 with the stored matrix, and it produces two impossible values. The median
gives 0.975 and it produces none. The two impossible values under the mode came
from NKG2C and NKG2A, which the quality table above flags as positive on 7.0
percent and 17.2 percent of events, so the failure and the diagnostic point at
the same two controls. Three configurations returned no usable estimate at all,
and the table records that instead of dropping the row.

The analysis therefore uses `method = "median"`, and
`ComputeSpilloverFromControls()` carries that as its default with this
measurement in its documentation. The rule to take away is narrower than "use
median". Use the mode when the controls are beads, and check the positive
fraction before you trust either.

### The computed matrix

```{r}
#| label: spillover-heatmap
#| fig-cap: "Spillover computed from the twelve single stained controls. The diagonal is dropped, because it is 1 everywhere and would set the colour scale."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("spillover_heatmap.png"))
```

```{r}
#| label: spillover-top

top <- ReadOutput("spillover_computed_top10.csv")
top$percent <- round(100 * top$spill, 2)
kable(
  top[, c("from", "to", "percent")],
  caption = "The ten largest computed spillover values.",
  col.names = c("From detector", "Into detector", "Spillover, percent")
)
```

### Computed against stored

```{r}
#| label: matrix-comparison

matrix_comparison <- ReadOutput("spillover_computed_vs_stored.csv")
kable(
  head(matrix_comparison, 10),
  digits = 2,
  caption = "The ten pairs where the computed matrix disagrees most with the stored one. All values are percentages.",
  col.names = c("From", "Into", "Computed", "Stored", "Difference, points")
)
```

The two matrices agree closely in the middle and they disagree at the top. The
largest gap is BV510 into the violet 450/50 detector. Both matrices agree that
this pair carries the largest spillover in the panel, and they disagree on its
size. That residual is worth naming rather than smoothing over. It is not
resolved here, and a real experiment would settle it by a plot of that one pair
before the choice of a matrix.

## Part 2: automated gating

The template mirrors the hierarchy that the authors published.

```{r}
#| label: template

template <- read.csv(
  file.path("..", "gating", "omip39_gating_template.csv"),
  check.names = FALSE
)
kable(
  template[, c("alias", "pop", "parent", "dims", "gating_method", "gating_args")],
  caption = "The gating template. Each row is one population."
)
```

The four quadrant populations are built differently from the way the analyst
built them. FlowJo drew one quadrant gate, which sets both cut points at once.
The template fits two one dimensional gates, on CD56 and on CD3 separately, and
it then combines them with a boolean. The populations are defined the same way
and the cut points are found independently, so a difference between the two
results can come from that alone.

```{r}
#| label: automated-tree
#| fig-cap: "The hierarchy the template produced."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("automated_tree.png"))
```

## Part 3: the comparison

The published workspace holds 163 populations, and most of them are boolean
combinations of six markers below the CD56dim branch. This comparison covers the
seven named parent populations, which is where a difference means something. The
mapping between the two naming schemes is a judgement, so it lives in a file.

```{r}
#| label: population-map

population_map <- read.csv(
  file.path("..", "gating", "omip39_population_map.csv"),
  check.names = FALSE
)
kable(
  population_map,
  caption = "How a manual population name maps to a template alias, and why."
)
```

```{r}
#| label: comparison

comparison <- ReadOutput("comparison.csv")
kable(
  comparison[, c("manual", "automated", "manual_percent", "automated_percent",
                 "difference", "verdict")],
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Manual against automated, percent of parent, on one donor file.",
  col.names = c("Manual", "Automated", "Manual, percent", "Automated, percent",
                "Difference, points", "Verdict")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: comparison-scatter
#| fig-cap: "Each population once. The dashed line is exact agreement."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("comparison_scatter.png"))
```

### Where they agree and where they do not

Four of the seven populations agree within five percentage points, a tolerance
that was set as a judgement before the numbers were read and that is not a
published standard. The disagreement is not spread evenly. It starts at the
singlet gate, where the analyst kept 96.5 percent of viable events and the
template kept 86.7 percent. `openCyto::singletGate` fits a regression of FSC-H
on FSC-A and cuts at a fixed distance from it, while the analyst drew a polygon
by eye and drew it wider. Everything below inherits that difference. The
template throws away roughly a tenth more events at the singlet step, and it
counts the populations below out of a smaller and slightly different parent. The
lymphocyte gate then differs by 5.7 points in the same direction. By the CD56
against CD3 split the two methods are close again on the small populations, at
2.5 points and 1.4 points, and further apart on the largest one at 6.0 points.

## Part 4: reproducing the paper

The comparison above asks whether two analyses of one file agree. It does not
ask whether the paper's conclusions hold. That is a different question, and the
deposited data can answer it. OMIP-039 makes seven directional claims about how
CD56dim NKG2C+ NK cells differ from CD56dim NKG2C- NK cells, and it states one
composite phenotype as prototypic for adaptive NK cells. Each claim is recorded
in a file with the sentence it came from, so a reader can check the claim
against the paper before the check of the number against the data.

```{r}
#| label: claims-file

claims <- read.csv(
  file.path("..", "gating", "omip39_paper_claims.csv"),
  check.names = FALSE
)
kable(
  claims[, c("claim_id", "marker", "measure", "direction", "figure")],
  caption = "The claims, as recorded. The quote column holds the sentence each one came from and is omitted here for width."
)
```

Each claim is tested twice, by two routes that share no gating decision.

### Route 1: the authors' own gates

The deposited workspace holds 64 boolean populations under each NKG2C branch,
which is Figure 1C. A boolean set partitions its parent, so the frequency of one
marker is the sum of the counts where that marker is positive. That derivation
uses only the gates the authors drew, and it adds nothing.

```{r}
#| label: claims-manual

claims_manual <- ReadOutput("claims_manual.csv")
kable(
  claims_manual[, c("marker", "direction", "test_percent", "reference_percent",
                    "difference_points", "verdict")],
  digits = 2,
  caption = "The paper's claims, tested against its own gates.",
  col.names = c("Marker", "Paper expects", "NKG2C+ percent", "NKG2C- percent",
                "Difference, points", "Verdict")
)
```

All six frequency claims hold, and the differences are large. NKG2A falls by
41.8 percentage points and ILT2 rises by 21.7.

### Figure 1C, the prototypic adaptive phenotype

```{r}
#| label: phenotype

phenotype <- ReadOutput("adaptive_phenotype_manual.csv")
kable(
  phenotype,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "The population NKG2A- NKp30- Siglec-7- ILT2+ CD57+ CD2+, in each NKG2C branch.",
  col.names = c("Branch", "Population", "Events", "Parent events",
                "Percent of parent")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: phenotype-enrichment
#| echo: false

enrichment <- phenotype$percent_of_parent[1] / phenotype$percent_of_parent[2]
cat(sprintf(
  "The prototypic phenotype is %.1f times as frequent in NKG2C+ as in NKG2C-.\n",
  enrichment
))
```

That ratio is the central claim of the paper, computed from the data that the
authors deposited alongside it.

### Route 2: the automated template

```{r}
#| label: claims-automated

claims_automated <- ReadOutput("claims_automated.csv")
kable(
  claims_automated[, c("marker", "direction", "test_percent", "reference_percent",
                       "difference_points", "verdict")],
  digits = 2,
  caption = "The same claims, tested against gates the template fitted from scratch.",
  col.names = c("Marker", "Paper expects", "NKG2C+ percent", "NKG2C- percent",
                "Difference, points", "Verdict")
)
```

Five of the six claims reproduce, with the same directions and comparable
magnitudes. The sixth does not, and the reason is a broken gate rather than a
failed claim. The automated NKp30 gate calls 100 percent of events positive in
both branches, so `mindensity` put its cut below the whole distribution. The
claim is reported as "too small to call" rather than dropped, because a silent
omission would read as agreement. That gate needs a bounded search range, and it
is not fixed yet.

```{r}
#| label: claims-plot
#| fig-cap: "Both routes. A bar is the difference in percent positive between the two NKG2C branches."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("claims_plot.png"))
```

## Part 5: clustering, a third route

Gating asks how many cells fall inside a boundary. Clustering asks how many
groups are in the data and what each one expresses. The second question needs no
hierarchy, so a population that nobody thought to gate can still appear. Gating
removes debris, dead cells and doublets first, and the clustering runs on the
lymphocyte gate only. A cluster of debris is not a finding, and it stretches the
embedding so that everything else is squeezed into a corner.

```{r}
#| label: umap-cell-types
#| fig-cap: "UMAP of the lymphocyte gate, coloured by the annotated cell type."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("umap_cell_types.png"))
```

### How a cluster gets a name

No cluster is named by eye. Each metacluster is scored against a definitions
file that gives the expected sign of each marker, and the best scoring
definition wins. The margin to the runner up is reported, so a close call is
visible.

```{r}
#| label: cluster-annotation

annotation <- ReadOutput("cluster_annotation.csv")
kable(
  annotation[, c("cluster", "events", "percent_of_total", "cell_type",
                 "runner_up", "margin")],
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Each metacluster, its label, and how close the second choice was.",
  col.names = c("Metacluster", "Events", "Percent of gate", "Label",
                "Runner up", "Margin")
)
```

The score is a weighted mean over the markers a definition names, and it is not
a sum. That distinction is not cosmetic. Under a sum, a definition is rewarded
for naming more markers alone. The adaptive NK definition names eight markers
and the T cell definition names two, so the adaptive label won every cluster,
including the one that holds 88 percent of the file. The mean removes that
effect.

```{r}
#| label: cluster-heatmap
#| fig-cap: "Median marker expression per metacluster, scaled within each marker. This table drives the annotation."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("cluster_heatmap.png"))
```

```{r}
#| label: umap-markers
#| fig-cap: "The same embedding, coloured by each lineage marker. Read the labels against these panels."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("umap_markers.png"))
```

### Three routes, one file

```{r}
#| label: three-way

three_way <- ReadOutput("three_way_comparison.csv")
kable(
  three_way[, c("cell_type", "manual_percent", "automated_percent",
                "clustering_percent")],
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Every number is a percentage of the lymphocyte gate, so the three columns are comparable.",
  col.names = c("Cell type", "Manual gating", "Automated gating", "Clustering")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: three-way-plot
#| fig-cap: "The same table as a figure."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("three_way_comparison.png"))
```

Clustering tracks automated gating closely on the largest population, and it
undercounts the small NK subsets. That is the expected failure mode. A rare
population is absorbed into a neighbouring metacluster, because the number of
metaclusters is chosen in advance and 12 is a guess. The three columns disagree
most where the population is smallest, which is also where the biology of this
paper sits. That result is worth stating plainly, rather than presenting the
agreement on T cells as though it settled the matter.

## Discussion: where the three routes disagree, and why

The table above is easy to read as three roughly similar answers. It is more
useful read as three specific disagreements, and each one has a different cause.

### The NK compartment is not where they disagree

Ask first how many NK cells there are, before you ask how to divide them.

```{r}
#| label: nk-total

nk_total <- ReadOutput("nk_compartment_total.csv")
kable(
  nk_total,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "CD56+ CD3- cells as a percentage of the lymphocyte gate.",
  col.names = c("Route", "NK cells, percent of lymphocytes")
)
```

Automated gating and clustering land within 0.13 percentage points of each
other, at 5.79 against 5.92, and they reached that number by completely
different means. One route fitted a boundary on two markers. The other route
grouped events in eight dimensions and it never saw a gate. Agreement between
two methods that share no machinery is worth more than agreement between two
runs of the same one. Manual gating puts the number 2.5 points higher, at 8.25.

### Disagreement 1: the CD3 cut point moves cells between compartments

The automated template calls 93.3 percent of lymphocytes CD3 positive. The
manual analysis assigns 85.1 percent to CD56- CD3+ and 3.6 percent to
CD56+ CD3+, so it calls 88.8 percent CD3 positive. A CD3 gate set 4.5 percentage
points lower does not lose cells; it moves them. The cells leave the NK
compartment and they arrive in the T cell compartment, which is exactly the
pattern in the table. T cells rise from 85.1 to 91.1, NKT-like cells fall from
3.6 to 2.2, and NK cells fall from 8.25 to 5.79.

`mindensity` puts its cut at the lowest density point between two peaks. On CD3
in this file the negative and positive populations are not cleanly separated, so
that point sits inside the shoulder of the positive distribution. The
consequence is that the largest population absorbs part of the smallest, which
is the direction that matters least for the T cell number and most for the NK
number.

### Disagreement 2: the bright and dim split is unreliable in both automated routes

This is the largest disagreement in the report, and neither automated route
handles it well.

| Route | CD56bright, percent of NK cells |
|---|---|
| Manual | no gate; the authors gate CD56dim directly |
| Automated gating | 1.9, which is 0.112 of 5.79 |
| Clustering | 51.7, which is 3.058 of 5.92 |

CD56bright NK cells are usually a small minority of blood NK cells, so a value
near 2 percent is low and a value above 50 percent is not credible. The two
automated routes fail in opposite directions on the same split. The automated
gate fails because CD56bright and CD56dim are one continuous distribution rather
than two separated peaks, so a density based cut has no clear minimum to find.
The clustering fails for a related reason. The definitions file scores CD56 with
a doubled weight for `high`, and any metacluster with above average CD56
attracts that label, bright or not. This is why the CD56dim subsets look as
though clustering lost them. It did not. The events are in the CD56bright label
instead, and the compartment total is intact.

### What follows for the paper's conclusions

None of the above changes the answer to the question that the paper asks. The
claims in Part 4 are about the ratio between two branches of the CD56dim
population, and every route that produced those branches at all gave the same
directions with comparable magnitudes. A cut point that moves the boundary
between two populations changes both of their frequencies. It does not reverse
the sign of a difference measured within one of them. That is why the six
directional claims survive a gating strategy that disagrees with the authors by
2.5 percentage points on the NK compartment.

### What this shows and what it does not

It shows that an automated template reaches the same conclusions as a published
expert analysis on a real panel, and it names the specific gates where the two
disagree and by how much. It does not show that any of the three methods is
right. There is no ground truth here, only three analyses of one file, and where
two routes agree and one differs, that is not a vote.

The report also says nothing about analyst to analyst variation, which is the
number that the literature reports. That number needs the same files gated by
many people. Maecker and colleagues did exactly that with 15 laboratories, and
they measured a mean CV of 20.5 percent under local gating against 4 percent
under central gating [2]. One donor file cannot reproduce that design.

What one file can show is where the fragility sits. The fragility is not in the
compensation, which two independent methods agreed on to 0.54 percentage points
once the right summary statistic was used, and it is not in the directional
claims, which survived every route. It is in two cut points on continuous
distributions, CD3 and CD56, where a small change in a boundary moves a large
number of cells. A gate on a bimodal marker holds steady. A gate on a continuum
is a decision, and a report should record it as one. In this repository it is
recorded. The cut sits in a CSV that a reviewer can read and a version control
system can diff.

## Reproducing this

```bash
# Pull this dataset only, not the 103 GB archive
./sync.sh pull datasets/flowrepository/OMIP-39

# Build the container. Every package version is pinned and asserted at build time.
./containers/build.sh

# The four analysis steps, in order
for step in 02_omip39_compensation_and_gating \
            03_compensation_method_sweep \
            04_omip39_reproduce_paper \
            05_omip39_clustering_umap; do
  podman run --rm -v "$PWD:/work:z" -w /work everything-flow-cytometry:latest \
    Rscript "scripts/${step}.R"
done

# This report
podman run --rm -v "$PWD:/work:z" -w /work everything-flow-cytometry:latest \
  quarto render reports/omip39_automated_gating.qmd
```

```{r}
#| label: session-info

sessionInfo()
```
